I feel Gary did break his Joker shell. IIRC his voice cracked for a split second after Gary's testimony about him being the only nice one. I don't quite get the rape scene either, but I feel that that took away the impact of the Gary scene. Take that out and it further emphasizes why he broke through the Joker persona for a split second, and it would have been a much stronger impact overall. Kind feels like the rape scene was added for shock value or a criticism of the prison system but that could have been done in a different way without being as distracting as it is now.
I kind of agree, but I'm really not satisfied, I hoped for more.

What rape scene? I saw the movie yesterday and didn’t miss a minute of the movie. Where do you live? Are there alternative edits out there like the spiderverse movie? Sorry just trying to understand what you’re making a key reference to.
it isn’t explicitly shown. it’s after the guards take arthur to the bathroom and he strips, then it cuts to him wearing just a shirt with heavily bruised butt and thighs.
Ohhhh. I thought that’s when it might’ve been. Just wanted to make sure. Thanks!
Yup

The role of Joker is a form of power fantasy for Arthur (and for his followers). The Gary testimony demonstrates the disastrous ramifications of Arthur’s past actions on someone he likes. Arthur though is too absorbed into the power fantasy of Joker to fully realize what Gary is telling him. Upon his return to Arkham he is raped and returned to a powerless position. The power Arthur felt from being Joker was in the end fantasy, since, as you said, he is returned to the same position that birthed Joker in the first place (indicating the failure of the role of Joker in meaningfully changing Arthur’s life).

Thank you for writing this out. This is exactly what I got from the inference that he was sexually assaulted by the guards. I think the Joker persona started to crack when his lawyer said Lee is lying to him (and she then admits it). Then he heard testimonies in court of people he actually cared about who were all in all very kind to him (Sophie and Gary) and it started to creep in that being Joker doesn’t feel as good as it used to. In fact, his  insults he makes as Joker earn the ire of people who have authority over him (guards) and they show him just how powerless he really is. The thing that pushed it over the top was his friend being killed. The other people he cared about, Sophie and Gary, had their lives negatively affected by Joker but now someone he liked was dead because of it. I believe it’s all of these things that eventually break him and make him realize the gravity of what he’s done.
So what, it was just a case of getting it thru his thick skull? All the abuse and punishment beforehand werent enough?

I think I kinda get it. Going full joker didn't happen again for a long while, and once it did he has his big day, and that very day ends with very direct consequences. also I didn't think about that guy getting murdered as his friend, they did focus a lot on Arthur while that guy was being murdered. 


I get what your saying, its all adding up, sophie, gary and then the rape culminating in showing him where he *is* and what his choices bore out.

Are you interested in an explanation of the scene or not? Is it really that baffling how being placed in what is among the most powerless positions someone can be placed in might make someone realize they aren’t this powerful Joker figure who “can do anything?” Arthur retreats into the fantasy of the Joker role to escape from the prior abuse and punishment. The return of that abuse and punishment in a particularly harsh form forces him back to reality and highlights the failure of the Joker fantasy (as it clearly didn’t succeed in having him escape such abuse).

Exactly. People left and right are saying Arthur confessed the Joker never existed because the guards "took it out of him" in the act of rape. But I believe it was the call out from Gary which woke him out of his fantasy world where everyone but him was to blame

Yeah I get it now. I think what was missing for me to understand was the proximity between the two, the "return" of the joker and then almost immediate return to powerlessness as well as the impact of the murder of his fellow inmate. Also how sophie and Gary didn't quite get there, but they did set the stage for him to manage a semblence of empathy.

The sexual assault isn’t the turning point, but it leads to one of them. There are a few moments where Arthur realizes that indulging the fantasy of the Joker is hurting other people in tangible, escalating ways. From traumatizing Puddles to getting the childlike inmate killed to inspiring a bombing. Arthur is a murderer but he’s not the complete monster that the prosecution portrays him as; he still has some moral lines and some understanding of the consequences of his actions. And that ties into the larger theme of the film; each main character wants to build a simplistic narrative around Arthur but none of them really fully fit him.

Also, you could see that scene as social commentary: Arthur uses violence and murder in a way that society sees as unacceptable, but the violence and murder and abuse that the prison guards use is tacitly, if not openly, accepted. That violence is all “according to plan”, as the Dark Knight’s Joker explained.

That is a really good point. It really shows the double standard of what we consider "acceptable" violence and what we consider "unacceptable" violence. Those guards, whatever they did to Arthur, will never face punishment. In our world it's "all part of the plan" to abuse inmates. The guards think Arthur and people like him "deserve it." Joker believed all the people he killed "deserved it" too - he wasn't just murdering people left and right, it was people he believed to be bad. The people in the position of authority are no better than Joker, they are just causing violence in an "acceptable" way.
It was hearing the murder of the kid singing "when the saints" that finished Joker in him.
